claims.feature: differentiation by diction and idiom, not accent
claims.claim: No vowel/consonant accent-marking is wanted; Orcs deliberately never drop aitches in the text; the linguistic differentiation Tolkien built is in diction and idiom.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 193 to Terence Tiller (2 Nov 1956)
claims.quote: in diction, idiom, and so on

claims.feature: Minas Tirith as the standard register
claims.claim: Minas Tirith is to the Common Speech as London is to modern English — the standard of comparison, whose people have no accent.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 193
claims.quote: as London is to modern English

claims.claim: The Rohirrim spoke with a slower tempo and more sonorous articulation than modern urbans, and in Common Speech speak the best Minas Tirith, perhaps a little too carefully as a learned tongue.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 193
claims.quote: a slower tempo and more sonorous articulation

claims.feature: Orcs nasty by delivery not vulgarism
claims.claim: Orcs are to sound nasty through intonation, articulation and tempo, not through conventional features of modern vulgar English.

claims.feature: reading, not drama (necklace on a thread)
claims.claim: The book needs the older art of the reading mime; dramatization flattens scenery and characters, whereas passages read as a necklace upon a thread of narration would be fairer.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 194 to Terence Tiller (6 Nov 1956)
claims.quote: as a necklace upon a thread of narration

claims.claim: The tale was conceived epically rather than dramatically, so dramatizing it without liberties strips setting from dialogue and leaves both flat.

claims.feature: verse triggers archaic style; no modern rusticity
claims.claim: A speaker who breaks into formal verse uses an archaic style as anyone capable of verse then would; where dialect marked place not rank, avoid any modern rusticity.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 152 to Rayner Heppenstall (22 Sept 1954)

claims.feature: miles are miles (literal geography and season)
claims.claim: Though a fairy-story, the tale takes place in this earth's northern hemisphere: miles, days and weather are literal, and seasons are pictorial and basic to the tone.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210 to Forrest J. Ackerman (June 1958)
claims.quote: miles are miles, days are days, and weather is weather

claims.feature: tone not to be lowered to childish fairy-tale
claims.claim: 'Old scamp!' exemplifies the treatment's tendency to lower the tone toward a childish fairy-tale; the setting is not fairy-land but real river-lands in autumn.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210

claims.feature: neither contes de fées nor scientification
claims.claim: Any pull toward French fairy-tale style or toward science-fiction diction ('food concentrate' for lembas) is alien to the story; both modes are rejected.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: Both modes are alien to my story

claims.feature: characters kept in style and sentiment
claims.claim: Speeches must represent the characters as written, in style and sentiment; perverting a character is resented more than spoiling plot or scenery.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210

claims.claim: Anticipating later devices and assimilating one incident to another have a flattening effect; a scene of gloom and silence beats yet another scene of screams and slashings.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210

claims.claim: The Ringbearers' action and the heroic matter are totally different in tone and scenery and must each be kept in coherent sequence; jumbling destroys both.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: totally different in tone and scenery

claims.claim: Rohan is a dwelling of Men in a heroic age: no private chambers, the king receiving on the dais of his hall — details must fit the world described.
claims.source: The Letters of J.R.R. Tolkien, no. 210
claims.quote: a dwelling of Men in an ‘heroic age’

claims.claim: Gandalf must not splutter: despite humour and an avuncular manner he is a person of high and noble authority and great dignity.
claims.quote: Gandalf was to be spluttering. Tolkien disapproved

verdicts.trueWording: in diction, idiom, and so on
verdicts.note: Letter 193 (PDF p.271) verbatim: 'no accent-differentiation is needed or desirable'; aitches 'not dropped in the text, and that is deliberate'; 'I paid great attention to such linguistic differentiation as was possible: in diction, idiom, and so on'. All three limbs on the page.

verdicts.trueWording: as London is to modern English, and the standard of comparison
verdicts.note: Letter 193 verbatim: 'As Minas Tirith is at the source of C. Speech it is to C.S. as London is to modern English, and the standard of comparison! None of its inhabitants should have an "accent" in terms of vowels &c.' Every limb supported.

verdicts.trueWording: a slower tempo and more sonorous articulation, than modern 'urbans'
verdicts.note: Letter 193 verbatim, plus 'speaking the best M[inas] T[irith]. Possibly a little too good, as it would be a learned language, somewhat slower and more careful than a native's.' Letter says they spoke their own tongue so 'at least'; claim does not contradict this.

verdicts.trueWording: intonation, articulation, and tempo ... to make Orcs sound nasty
verdicts.note: Wayback capture 20260108020555 of tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Letter_193 (live host 403s). Quote verbatim. The page instantiates the vulgar-English limb narrowly as 'Orcs should not drop aitches; that was not done in the text, deliberately' — the general phrase 'vulgar English' is not on the page, but the contrast the claim makes is.

verdicts.trueWording: as a necklace upon a thread of narration
verdicts.note: Letter 194 (PDF p.272) verbatim: 'it requires rather the older art of the reading "mime"'; 'both the "scenery" and the "characters" become flat'; the necklace passage 'would ... prove both more interesting to listeners, and fairer to the author'. All limbs supported.

Wayback capture 20260110041608 of tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Letter_194 (live host 403s). Quote verbatim; the page also carries 'dialogue with the settings removed' and 'Both the scenery and the characters had become flat'. But the Gateway summary omits Tolkien's conditional entirely — the word 'libert' does not occur on the page (machine-checked). That limb IS in the underlying Letter 194: 'unless the dramatizer is given or takes liberties, as an independent person' — so the claim is true of the letter, just not fully carried by the cited page.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: the 'unless the dramatizer is given or takes liberties' condition — absent from the Tolkien Gateway page

verdicts.trueWording: it would be best to avoid any modern rusticity
verdicts.note: Letter 152 to Rayner Heppenstall, 22 Sept 1954 (PDF p.205) verbatim: 'The young minstrel bursts into formal verse, and so uses an archaic style - as anyone would capable of verse at the time'; 'in a period when "dialect" merely marked place and not rank or function ... it would be best to avoid any modern rusticity.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: miles are miles, days are days, and weather is weather
verdicts.note: Letter 210 (PDF p.291) verbatim, preceded by 'The Lord of the Rings may be a "fairy-story", but it takes place in the Northern hemisphere of this earth'. Seasons limb: 'They are pictorial ... this is basic to the purport and tone of the tale.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: We are not in 'fairy-land', but in real river-lands in autumn
verdicts.note: Letter 210 (PDF p.292) verbatim; the 'Old scamp!' limb is verbatim too: 'This is a good example of the general tendency that I find in Z to reduce and lower the tone towards that of a more childish fairy-tale.' Both limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: Both modes are alien to my story
verdicts.note: Letter 210 verbatim: lembas 'called a "food concentrate"'; 'I dislike strongly any pulling of my tale towards the style and feature of "contes des fees", or French fairy-stories. I dislike equally any pull towards "scientification", of which this expression is an example. Both modes are alien to my story.' The book prints 'contes des fees' (claim's header spells it 'contes de fees'); no substantive divergence.

verdicts.trueWording: represented as I have presented them: in style and sentiment
verdicts.note: Letter 210 verbatim, including the second limb: 'I should resent perversion of the characters ... even more than the spoiling of the plot and scenery.' Both limbs supported.

Letter 210 verbatim; assimilation limb verbatim as 'the flattening effect that assimilation of one incident to another must have'; the preference limb as 'A scene of gloom lit by a small red fire ... would seem to me far more impressive than yet one more scene of screams and rather meaningless slashings'. 'Silence' is supported in the same item: 'The Black Riders do not scream, but keep a more terrifying silence.'

verdicts.trueWording: totally different in tone and scenery
verdicts.note: Letter 210 (PDF pp.293-294) verbatim: 'Prime Action, the Ringbearers ... Subsidiary Action ... leading to the "heroic" matter. It is essential that these two branches should each be treated in coherent sequence ... because they are totally different in tone and scenery. Jumbling them together entirely destroys these things.' All limbs supported.

verdicts.trueWording: a dwelling of Men in an 'heroic age'
verdicts.note: Letter 210 (PDF p.294) verbatim: 'In such a time private "chambers" played no part ... He received guests or emissaries, seated on the dais in his royal hall.' The passage is about Theoden/Edoras, i.e. Rohan ('the "heroic" Rohirrim'). The 'fit the world described' limb is verbatim in the same letter at item 8: 'If details are to be added ... they should at least fit the world described.'

verdicts.trueWording: Gandalf was to be spluttering. Tolkien disapproved both
verdicts.note: Wayback capture 20260820023126 of tolkiengateway.net/wiki/Letter_210 (live host 403s). Quote verbatim as the leading substring of 'Gandalf was to be spluttering. Tolkien disapproved both.' But the page carries none of the dignity limb: machine-checked, the strings 'dignity', 'avuncular', 'noble authority' and 'humour' do not occur anywhere on the page. That limb IS in the underlying Letter 210 ('he is a person of high and noble authority, and great dignity'), so the claim is true of the letter but not fully carried by the cited page.
verdicts.unsupportedLimb: 'despite humour and an avuncular manner he is a person of high and noble authority and great dignity' — absent from the Tolkien Gateway page
